title: BPC-157 vs TB-500
summary: BPC-157 and TB-500 are the two peptides most often discussed for soft-tissue healing and most often combined. They are not alternatives within one class: BPC-157 is a fragment of a gastric-juice protein proposed to act through nitric-oxide and growth-factor signalling, while TB-500 is a fragment of thymosin beta-4, an actin-binding protein involved in cell migration. One indexed study compares them directly: a 2026 rat study of Achilles tendon healing that tested each and the pair, reporting higher load to failure in the treated groups than in controls. Neither compound is approved; BPC-157 is prohibited in sport under WADA S0 and TB-500 under S2.

faq.question: Is BPC-157 or TB-500 better for tendons?
faq.answer: Neither has controlled human evidence for tendon healing. One 2026 rat study tested both and found effects in treated groups versus controls without ranking them. The question has no evidence-based answer yet.

faq.question: Can BPC-157 and TB-500 be used together?
faq.answer: Communities do, as the Wolverine stack. One rat study tested the pair; no human study has. The stack page holds what exists.

faq.question: What is the main difference between them?
faq.answer: Origin and mechanism. BPC-157 is a gastric-protein fragment acting through nitric-oxide and growth-factor signalling; TB-500 is a thymosin β4 fragment acting through actin binding and cell migration.

faq.question: Which has more human research?
faq.answer: Thymosin β4, TB-500's parent protein, has been in several human trials in eye and skin conditions; the TB-500 fragment itself has very little. BPC-157 has three small uncontrolled pilots from one clinic.

faq.question: Are both banned in sport?
faq.answer: Yes. BPC-157 under WADA S0 and TB-500 under S2, both prohibited at all times.

open_questions: No human study compares the two for any outcome.
Whether the marketed TB-500 fragment behaves like full thymosin β4 is untested.
The one animal comparison did not establish that either outperforms the other.

guide.heading: BPC-157 vs TB-500 in two minutes
guide.html:
Different molecules, different proposed mechanisms. BPC-157 comes from a stomach protein and is studied for gut, tendon, muscle and nerve healing, almost all in rats. TB-500 is a piece of thymosin beta-4, a protein present in nearly every human cell that helps cells move; its parent molecule has been in human trials for eye and skin wounds.

Evidence. BPC-157: 228 publications, zero randomized trials, three uncontrolled human pilots from one clinic. TB-500 and thymosin beta-4 together: more than a thousand publications, several human trials of the parent protein, little on the marketed fragment itself.

Head to head. One rat tendon study in 2026 tested both.{{cite:pmid-42542926}} Nothing in people compares them.

Which is "better" is not a question the evidence can answer; they have not been tested for the same outcome in people, and the one animal study did not rank them.

guide.heading: BPC-157 vs TB-500 side effects: what has been reported in people
guide.lede: Neither has a controlled human safety record. What exists is small, and it is not the same molecule on both sides.
guide.html:
BPC-157. The only human safety data on record is a 2025 pilot in which 2 healthy adults were given BPC-157 into a vein, at up to 20 mg, with no control group. No side effects were reported.{{cite:pmid-40131143}} Two people cannot show that a compound is safe; they can only show that nothing obvious happened to them. The theoretical concern most often raised, that a compound which promotes new blood vessels might also feed a tumour, has not been tested in either direction.

TB-500. No human study has given the TB-500 fragment by injection, so it has no human side-effect record at all. The human trials belong to the full thymosin beta-4 protein. Two of them gave it into a vein to healthy volunteers and tracked how blood levels rose with the dose{{cite:pmid-20536472}}{{cite:pmid-34346165}}, and a 2025 randomized trial gave it to 96 heart attack patients.{{cite:pmid-41229390}} Those findings describe the full protein, not the fragment sold as TB-500.

So the honest comparison is two people on one side and none on the other, with the parent protein's trials standing in for a molecule they did not test.

guide.heading: BPC-157 vs TB-500 dosage: what the studies gave
guide.lede: Every figure here is a dose a study administered, reported as published. None is a suggestion, and animal doses do not convert into human ones.
guide.html:
The one study of both. In the 2026 rat tendon study, groups of eight rats received BPC-157 at 10 µg/kg a day, TB-500 at 60 µg/kg a day, both together, or nothing.{{cite:pmid-42542926}}

BPC-157 elsewhere. In people, the only dose on record is the single intravenous infusion of up to 20 mg in the 2-person pilot.{{cite:pmid-40131143}} In rats, the research group behind most of the literature commonly uses 10 µg/kg or 10 ng/kg; in its 2025 muscle-reattachment study, both doses were given by mouth daily.{{cite:pmid-39861766}}

Thymosin beta-4, the parent protein. A 2021 phase 1 trial gave healthy volunteers 0.5, 2.0 or 5.0 µg/kg into a vein once a day for 10 days.{{cite:pmid-34346165}} That is the full protein by infusion, which is not how TB-500 is used.

The figures that circulate for each compound appear in the comparison table above as commonly reported use. None of them has been tested in a trial. The dosage calculators convert a dose into syringe units; they do not choose one.

guide.heading: BPC-157 vs TB-500 cycle length: how long studies gave each one
guide.lede: Studies report treatment periods, not cycles. These are the periods on record.
guide.html:
BPC-157. Human data is a single infusion.{{cite:pmid-40131143}} In rats, healing was assessed at 28 and 42 days after muscle-tendon injury{{cite:pmid-34829776}}, reattached muscle was followed for 3 months{{cite:pmid-39861766}}, and recovery after spinal cord injury was reported as lasting a year.{{cite:pmid-35678659}} Those are follow-up periods in rats, not human courses.

TB-500 and thymosin beta-4. The rat tendon study measured strength at four weeks.{{cite:pmid-42542926}} The full protein's human trials ran 10 days of daily infusions followed for 28 days{{cite:pmid-34346165}}, 14 days of daily infusions{{cite:pmid-20536472}}, 56 days of eye drops including follow-up{{cite:pmid-25826322}}, and a skin-ulcer trial designed for 84 days of treatment.{{cite:pmid-17495250}}

Every compound's study durations, side by side, are on the peptide cycle length page.

guide.heading: Who should avoid BPC-157 or TB-500?
guide.lede: No trial or label defines it for either compound. Two facts on record still matter.
guide.html:
Neither compound has an approved label, and no trial of either lists exclusion criteria this page can cite, so there is no evidence-based list of who should avoid them. That is an absence of evidence, not a sign that they suit everyone.

Athletes. The U.S. Anti-Doping Agency states that BPC-157 is prohibited under the S0 category of the WADA Prohibited List{{cite:usada-bpc-157-prohibited}}, and TB-500 is named under S2. Both are prohibited at all times, in and out of competition.

Approval. USADA also states that BPC-157 is not approved for human use by the FDA or any other health authority.{{cite:usada-bpc-157-prohibited}} Neither TB-500 nor the full thymosin beta-4 protein holds a marketing authorisation anywhere.

What each record holds on safety is on the BPC-157 and TB-500 pages.

guide.heading: How the two are discussed as choices, and why the evidence cannot decide
guide.html: Communities frame BPC-157 as the local, targeted compound for a specific injury and TB-500 as the systemic one for diffuse or multiple injuries, which follows from their proposed mechanisms and dosing patterns rather than from any comparison. Both have been described for the same outcomes in animals.{{cite:pmid-42542926}} In people, BPC-157 has three uncontrolled pilots and TB-500's fragment has essentially nothing; thymosin β4's human trials used the full protein in eye drops and gels, a different molecule by size and route. A reader weighing the two is weighing two different kinds of gap, not two bodies of evidence. The Wolverine stack page covers the combination.
